#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -eu

# Send the projector power code over the GPIO IR transmitter.
LIRC_DEV="${LIRC_DEV:-/dev/lirc0}"
SCANCODE="${SCANCODE:-nec:0xa8}"
REPEATS="${1:-3}"
GAP_SECS="${GAP_SECS:-0.25}"

if [ ! -e "$LIRC_DEV" ]; then
  echo "IR TX device not found: $LIRC_DEV" >&2
  exit 1
fi

echo "Sending $SCANCODE on $LIRC_DEV ($REPEATS times)..."
i=1
while [ "$i" -le "$REPEATS" ]; do
  ir-ctl -d "$LIRC_DEV" -S "$SCANCODE"
  echo "Sent $i/$REPEATS"
  i=$((i + 1))
  if [ "$i" -le "$REPEATS" ]; then

Boot-time IR wake automation is now in place and tested.

What I implemented:
1. Added reusable IR wake script: [ada/bin/projector-ir-wake.sh](ada/bin/projector-ir-wake.sh#L1)
2. Added boot oneshot service: [systemd/system/projector-ir-wake.service](systemd/system/projector-ir-wake.service#L1)
3. Added Makefile test/control targets: [ada/Makefile](ada/Makefile#L74)

What it does:
1. Sends NEC power scancode 0xa8 via TX device /dev/lirc0.
2. Sends it 3 times by default on boot.
3. Supports manual one-shot and 3x testing through make.

Make targets added:
1. projector-on: [ada/Makefile](ada/Makefile#L76)
2. projector-once: [ada/Makefile](ada/Makefile#L80)
3. projector-boot-enable: [ada/Makefile](ada/Makefile#L84)
4. projector-boot-disable: [ada/Makefile](ada/Makefile#L89)
5. projector-boot-run: [ada/Makefile](ada/Makefile#L93)
6. projector-boot-status: [ada/Makefile](ada/Makefile#L97)

Validation performed:
1. Confirmed TX device capabilities on /dev/lirc0 (send supported, receive not supported).
2. Ran make projector-once successfully: sent 1/1.
3. Enabled and started service successfully.
4. Service run log shows successful sends: Sent 1/3, Sent 2/3, Sent 3/3, exit status 0.

If you want, I can also add a startup delay (for example 10-20 seconds) in [ada/bin/projector-ir-wake.sh](ada/bin/projector-ir-wake.sh#L1) in case the projector misses very early boot-time IR.

Usage: ir-ctl [OPTION...] --features
  or:  ir-ctl [OPTION...] --receive [save to file]
  or:  ir-ctl [OPTION...] --send [file to send]
  or:  ir-ctl [OPTION...] --scancode [scancode to send]
  or:  ir-ctl [OPTION...] --keycode [keycode to send]
  or:  ir-ctl [OPTION...] [to set lirc option]

Receive IR, send IR and list features of lirc device
You will need permission on /dev/lirc for the program to work

On the options below, the arguments are:
  DEV      - the /dev/lirc* device to use
  FILE     - a text file containing pulses and spaces
  CARRIER  - the carrier frequency to use for sending
  DUTY     - the duty cycle to use for sending
  EMITTERS - comma separated list of emitters to use for sending, e.g. 1,2
  GAP      - gap between sending in microseconds
  RANGE    - set range of accepted carrier frequencies, e.g. 20000-40000
  TIMEOUT  - set length of space before receiving stops in microseconds
  KEYCODE  - key code in keymap
  SCANCODE - protocol:scancode, e.g. nec:0xa814
  KEYMAP   - a rc keymap file from which to send keys

Note that most lirc setting have global state, i.e. the device will remain
in this state until set otherwise.

  -d, --device=DEV           lirc device to use
  -f, --features             list lirc device features
  -K, --keycode=KEYCODE      send IR keycode from keymap
  -r, --receive[=FILE]       receive IR to stdout or file
  -s, --send=FILE            send IR pulse and space file
  -S, --scancode=SCANCODE    send IR scancode in protocol specified
  -v, --verbose              verbose output

 Receiving options:
  -1, --one-shot             end receiving after first message
      --mode2                output in mode2 format
  -m, --measure-carrier      report carrier frequency
  -M, --no-measure-carrier   disable reporting carrier frequency
  -n, --narrowband           use narrowband receiver, disable learning mode
  -R, --carrier-range=RANGE  set receiver carrier range
  -t, --timeout=TIMEOUT      set receiving timeout
  -w, --wideband             use wideband receiver aka learning mode

 Sending options:
  -c, --carrier=CARRIER      set send carrier
  -D, --duty-cycle=DUTY      set send duty cycle
  -e, --emitters=EMITTERS    set send emitters
  -g, --gap=GAP              set gap between files or scancodes
  -k, --keymap=KEYMAP        use keymap to send key from

  -?, --help                 Give this help list
      --usage                Give a short usage message
  -V, --version              Print program version

Mandatory or optional arguments to long options are also mandatory or optional
for any corresponding short options.

response.value:
Perfect way to verify it yourself after a reboot:

1. Check if it is enabled for boot
Run:
sudo systemctl is-enabled projector-ir-wake.service

How to read it:
enabled = it is wired to start at boot
disabled = it will not auto-run

2. Check logs from the current boot
Run:
sudo journalctl -u projector-ir-wake.service -b --no-pager

How to read it:
You want to see lines like:
Starting projector-ir-wake.service
Sending nec:0xa8 on /dev/lirc0 (3 times)
Sent 1/3, Sent 2/3, Sent 3/3
Finished projector-ir-wake.service

3. Check service result snapshot
Run:
sudo systemctl status projector-ir-wake.service --no-pager -l

How to read it for a oneshot service:
Active: inactive (dead) is normal after it finishes
Look for status=0/SUCCESS and Result: success

4. Confirm timing matches this boot
Run:
sudo systemctl show projector-ir-wake.service -p ActiveEnterTimestamp -p InactiveEnterTimestamp -p Result -p ExecMainStatus

How to read it:
Timestamps should be shortly after boot
Result should be success
ExecMainStatus should be 0

5. If you want to inspect the previous boot too
Run:
sudo journalctl -u projector-ir-wake.service -b -1 --no-pager

Yes, heliocron is a good fit here.

For your goal, the simplest pattern is:
1. Cron starts a job once per day (for example at noon).
2. That job waits until sunset using heliocron, then sends your IR on code.
3. Separate normal cron entries handle off times (10pm weekdays, midnight weekends).

Minimal example:

    CRON_TZ=America/New_York
    0 12 * * * /usr/local/bin/heliocron -l YOUR_LAT -o YOUR_LON wait -e sunset --run-missed-task &&

3 >> /tmp/projector-cron.log 2>&1

    0 0 * * 6,0 /usr/bin/ir-ctl -d /dev/lirc0 -S nec:0xa8 >> /tmp/projector-cron.log 2>&1

1. CRON_TZ makes schedule interpretation explicit for US East Coast.
2. --run-missed-task helps if the Pi was down and comes back after sunset.
3. The off lines above use the same code; that only works safely if your projector power command is true OFF (not toggle).
4. If 0xa8 is a toggle, we should scan/find a discrete OFF code first, otherwise scheduled off can accidentally turn it on.

Yes, heliocron is a good fit here.

For your goal, the simplest pattern is:
1. Cron starts a job once per day (for example at noon).
2. That job waits until sunset using heliocron, then sends your IR on code.
3. Separate normal cron entries handle off times (10pm weekdays, midnight weekends).

Minimal example:

    CRON_TZ=America/New_York
    0 12 * * * /usr/local/bin/heliocron -l YOUR_LAT -o YOUR_LON wait -e sunset --run-missed-task && /home/ada/bin/projector-ir-wake.sh 3 >> /tmp/projector-cron.log 2>&1
    0 22 * * 1-5 /usr/bin/ir-ctl -d /dev/lirc0 -S nec:0xa8 >> /tmp/projector-cron.log 2>&1
    0 0 * * 6,0 /usr/bin/ir-ctl -d /dev/lirc0 -S nec:0xa8 >> /tmp/projector-cron.log 2>&1

Notes to learn from:
1. CRON_TZ makes schedule interpretation explicit for US East Coast.
2. --run-missed-task helps if the Pi was down and comes back after sunset.
3. The off lines above use the same code; that only works safely if your projector power command is true OFF (not toggle).
4. If 0xa8 is a toggle, we should scan/find a discrete OFF code first, otherwise scheduled off can accidentally turn it on.

### Delay execution of a command relative to sunrise or sunset

Permalink: Delay execution of a command relative to sunrise or sunset
The following code snippet entered into the terminal will wait until sunset on
25th Feb 2020 at the Royal Greenwich Observatory (17:32:17 +00:00) before listing
the files and folders contained within the user's home directory.

  $ heliocron --date 2020-02-25 --latitude 51.4769 --longitude -0.0005 \
wait --event sunset && ls ~
Thread going to sleep for _ seconds until 2020-02-25 17:32:17 +00:00. Press ctrl+C to cancel.
Integration with `cron` for recurring tasks is easy. The following snippet shows a `crontab` entry which will run every morning at 2am. `heliocron` will wait until 30 minutes before sunrise, before allowing the execution of the
`turn-on-lights.sh` script.

### The chosen event does not occur on the given day

Permalink: The chosen event does not occur on the given day
Sometimes, a particular event will never happen on a certain day at a certain
location. For example, the Sun never drops below 18° below the horizon in England
during the height of summer; astronomical dawn and dusk never occur.


When using the `report` subcommand, this is identified like so:

  $ heliocron -d 2020-06-21 -l 52.8300 -o 0.5135 report
<-- snip -->
Astronomical dawn is at:  Never
Astronomical dusk is at:  Never
When using the `wait` subcommand, an error is raised and the program terminates immediately:

  $ heliocron -d 2020-06-21 -l 52.8300 -o 0.5135 wait -e astronomical_dusk
Runtime error: The chosen event does not occur on this
day.

message.text: can we add a cron job that turns the projector on at sunset (us east coast) and off again at 10pm on the weekdays and midnight on weekends?

can we add a cron job that turns the projector on at sunset (us east coast) and off again at 10pm on the weekdays and midnight on weekends?

simple as possible, minimal lines of code. I want to learn, not build a production ready product

response.value:
In cron, 0 12 * * * means run at 12:00 PM (noon) every day.

Field-by-field:
1. 0 = minute
2. 12 = hour (24-hour clock)
3. * = every day of month
4. * = every month
5. * = every day of week

So it triggers daily at noon. If you set CRON_TZ=America/New_York, that noon is Eastern time.

response.value:
Short answer: no, do not install Rust with rustup as root for this.

Best practice:
1. Install Rust as your normal user account.
2. If needed system-wide, copy just the built binary into /usr/local/bin with sudo.

Why:
1. Root install puts everything under /root/.cargo and /root/.rustup.
2. That is awkward for updates, permissions, and reuse from your user shell.
3. You only need elevated privileges when placing final binaries or editing root cron/system files.

What to do right now:
1. In that installer prompt, choose 3 (Cancel).
2. Re-run rustup as your normal user.
3. After installing heliocron, promote the binary once with sudo install.

If you want simplest of all, skip Rust entirely and use the precompiled heliocron binary for Raspberry Pi 5 (aarch64).

message.text: is it a problem if i do all my dev work through a root ssh shell? it's just convient for editing boot files

response.value:
It is workable, but yes, it is a real footgun.

Main risks of doing daily dev as root:
1. One typo can damage the system instantly.
2. New files end up root-owned, then your normal user cannot edit/run them cleanly.
3. Build tools and package installs can pollute system locations and make debugging harder.
4. Scripts may accidentally rely on root-only behavior and later fail under normal users.
5. SSH as root increases blast radius if keys or session security ever go wrong.

Simple setup that keeps convenience:
1. Do normal coding as your user.
2. Use sudo only for privileged actions: service changes, boot config edits, package install.
3. For editing privileged files, use sudoedit (best) or edit as user then copy with sudo install.
4. Keep root shell for short admin tasks only, not your default dev session.

Good compromise pattern:
1. User shell for everything by default.
2. Separate root shell tab only when needed.
3. Immediately exit root shell after the admin change.

If you want, I can give you a tiny “safe workflow cheat sheet” for your Pi with 6-8 commands you can memorize.
